summary: Defines a PCEP extension that associates two or more LSPs so they act as working and protection paths for one another under an active stateful PCE. This lets a controller set up and manage backup paths that take over if the primary path fails.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8745 lets a path computer and its routers record which paths protect which. Two or more label switched paths are put in a group, called a path protection association group. One of them is the working path and the others are protection paths, and each member says which role it has and what kind of protection it uses, so that the router can signal the backup path when the working one fails.

questions: how to associate working and protection lsps in pcep
what is path protection association in pcep
what is a path protection association group
subtitle: A way for a PCE and its routers to group a working LSP with its protection LSPs so backups can be planned and controlled together.

tldr.problem: When a stateful PCE controls a working LSP, it is useful for the same PCE to compute and control the protection LSPs that take over when it fails. PCEP needed a way to say which LSPs protect which.
tldr.mechanism: It defines the Path Protection Association type (value 1) for the generic ASSOCIATION object, and a Path Protection Association TLV (type 38) whose flags mark each LSP as working or protection, primary or secondary, and give the protection type.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. PCCs and PCEs can now report, create and update a protection group, and reject malformed groups with defined errors.

today: RFC 8745 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756, so read the two together. The text of this RFC does not say how widely it is deployed.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 5440 describes the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) for communication between a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a PCE, or between a pair of PCEs. A PCE computes paths for MPLS-TE label switched paths from various constraints and optimization criteria.

Stateful PCE, specified in RFC 8231, adds the PCEP extensions that allow stateful control of paths between and across PCEP sessions. It includes mechanisms for LSP state synchronization, delegation of control of LSPs to the PCE, and PCE control of the timing and sequence of path computations. The focus is on a model where the LSPs are configured on the client and control over them is delegated to the stateful PCE, and RFC 8281 adds a mechanism to instantiate LSPs on a client at the request of a stateful PCE or a controller.

Path protection, described in RFC 4427, is the paradigm in which a working LSP is protected by one or more protection LSPs, which are activated when the working LSP fails. When the working LSP is computed and controlled by a PCE, there is a benefit in having the protection LSPs computed and controlled by the same PCE. This document specifies a stateful PCEP extension that associates two or more LSPs for that purpose, and it covers three cases: a client that creates a protection LSP and keeps control of it, reporting the association to the PCE afterwards; a client that creates the protection LSP and delegates control to a stateful PCE, including the association group in the delegation; and a protection LSP initiated by the stateful PCE itself, which keeps control of it.

A protection LSP can be established before the failure, in which case it is said to be in standby mode or to be a primary LSP, or after the failure of the working LSP, when it is known as a secondary LSP. Which of the two an operator chooses is a matter of choice or policy.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateful path computer keeps control of the paths it manages. When it manages a working path, it is useful for it to manage the backup path too, so that the backup is ready when the working path fails. This RFC gives PCEP the means to record that two paths are related in this way.

sections.title: The Path Protection Association Type
sections.content:
In RFC 8697, LSPs are not associated by listing the other LSPs they interact with, but by making them belong to an association group. All LSPs join an association group individually, and the generic ASSOCIATION object associates two or more of them. This document defines a new association type, the Path Protection Association Type, of value 1, and the corresponding group is the Path Protection Association Group (PPAG).

A member LSP of a PPAG can take the role of working LSP or protection LSP, and a PPAG can have one working LSP and/or one or more protection LSPs. The source, destination, Tunnel ID as carried in the LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV, and Protection Type of all LSPs within a PPAG must be the same. The Tunnel ID matters because, as described in RFC 3209, a TE tunnel associates a set of LSPs during a reroute or to spread a traffic trunk over multiple paths.

The association type is dynamic: the PCC or the PCE creates it for the LSPs of the same TE tunnel that originate at the same head node and terminate at the same destination. The association is conveyed to the peer in PCEP messages, and the association source is set to the address of the local PCEP speaker that created it, unless local policy says otherwise. An operator-configured Association Range must not be set for this association type and must be ignored.

RFC 8697 defines an ASSOC-Type-List TLV in the OPEN object for advertising which association types a speaker supports. That exchange for the Path Protection Association Type may be done before the association is used, so a speaker may include the type value 1 in the list before using a PPAG in PCEP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The grouping works by membership, not by pointing one path at another: each path joins the group on its own. Every path in the group must start and end in the same place and belong to the same traffic engineering tunnel, so that they are genuine alternatives for the same traffic. The group is created by whichever end builds the paths, and it is dynamic, so it comes and goes with the paths.

sections.title: The Path Protection Association TLV
sections.content:
The Path Protection Association TLV is an optional TLV for use in the ASSOCIATION object with the Path Protection Association Type. It must not be present more than once; if it appears more than once, only the first occurrence is processed and the others are ignored. It follows the PCEP TLV format of RFC 5440.

The Type field of the TLV is 38 and the Length field has a fixed value of 4. The value is a single 32-bit field of Path Protection Association Flags, where each bit is one option. The Protecting flag (P) is 1 bit and indicates whether the LSP is a working LSP, when it is 0, or a protection LSP, when it is 1. The Secondary flag (S) is 1 bit and indicates whether the LSP is a primary LSP, when it is 0, or a secondary LSP, when it is 1; the S flag is ignored if the P flag is not set. The Protection Type (PT) field is 6 bits and gives the LSP protection type in use, as defined in Section 14.1 of RFC 4872 in its LSP Protection Type Flags; any type already defined or later defined for the RSVP-TE PROTECTION object is acceptable unless stated otherwise. The unassigned bits are reserved, must be set to 0 on transmission and must be ignored on receipt.

If the TLV is missing from the PPAG ASSOCIATION object, the LSP is taken to be a working LSP, as if the P bit were unset.
sections.plainLanguage: Each path in the group carries a small set of flags. One says whether the path is the working one or the spare. One says whether the spare was set up before or after the failure. Six bits give the kind of protection in use, taken from the same list the RSVP-TE signalling uses. A path with no such flags at all counts as a working path.

sections.title: Operating the Association
sections.content:
An LSP is associated with the other LSPs it interacts with by adding them to a common association group through the ASSOCIATION object, with all the procedures and error handling of RFC 8697.

During state synchronization, a client reports all the existing LSP states as described in RFC 8231, and the association group membership of each LSP is reported as well, including PPAGs.

A client can associate a set of LSPs under its control for path protection, and can remove one or more of them from the corresponding group. In both cases it reports the change to the PCE with a Path Computation Report message. A client can also delegate the working and protection LSPs to an active stateful PCE, and the PCE can then update the paths and attributes of the LSPs in the group with a Path Computation Update message. A PCE can update the association to the client with the same kind of message. It is expected that both the working and the protection LSPs are delegated together, and to the same PCE, to avoid race conditions.

A PCE can create and update working and protection LSPs independently. Association groups can be created by both the PCE and the client, and a PCE can remove a protection LSP from a group. The PCE uses update or initiate messages to tell the client about the association.

When a PCEP session is terminated, the association information is cleared along with the LSP state information. After the State Timeout Interval expires at the client, the LSP state of that session reverts to operator-defined default parameters or behaviour, and the same is done for the association information. On termination at the PCE, the association information is cleared when the state reported by the client is cleared. Where an association group has no LSPs left in it, the association is considered deleted.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and the path computer exchange the membership of the group as part of the normal state reports and update messages. A client can add a path to the group, take one out, or hand the whole group over to the path computer, which is expected to take both the working path and its backup together so that they cannot disagree. When the session ends, the group information is cleared along with the path state.

sections.title: Errors
sections.content:
If a PCEP speaker does not support the Path Protection Association Type, it returns a PCEP error with Error-Type 26, Association Error, and Error-Value 1, association type is not supported.

All LSPs in a PPAG must belong to the same TE tunnel and have the same source and destination. If a speaker tries to add or update an LSP whose Tunnel ID, source or destination differs from the LSPs already in the group, it must send Error-Type 26 with Error-Value 9, tunnel ID or endpoints mismatch for path protection association. If the Protection Type differs from the LSPs in the group, it must send Error-Type 26 with Error-Value 6, association information mismatch. When the peer does not support the protection type set in the group, it must send Error-Type 26 with Error-Value 11, protection type is not supported.

An LSP may belong to more than one PPAG. If two of those groups conflict, the peer must send Error-Type 26 with Error-Value 6.

When the protection type is set to 1+1, which is 0x08 or 0x10, there may be at most one working LSP and one protection LSP in a group. When the protection type is set to 1:N, which is 0x04, there may be at most one protection LSP and no more than N working LSPs. An attempt to add another working or protection LSP beyond those limits must be answered with Error-Type 26 and Error-Value 10. During the make-before-break procedure, when two paths briefly coexist, the rule about the number of LSPs in a group must not be applied.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are checked and refused with a named error. A path with the wrong endpoints or the wrong tunnel cannot join the group. A path with a different kind of protection cannot join either. And a group cannot hold more paths than its protection type allows: one working path and one spare for the 1+1 type, or one spare and a set number of working paths for the 1:N type.

sections.title: Other Considerations
sections.content:
The working and protection LSPs are typically resource disjoint, for example node and shared risk link group disjoint, so that a single failure does not affect both. That disjointness requirement is handled through a separate association type, the Disjointness Association, and the diversity requirements for the protection LSP are met by including both association objects, one for the protection group and one for the disjointness group.

RFC 4872 introduces the concept and mechanisms for associating one LSP to another LSP across different RSVP-TE sessions, using the ASSOCIATION and PROTECTION objects. The information in the Path Protection Association TLV that a client receives from the PCE is used to trigger the signalling of the working and protection LSPs, with the Path Protection Association Flags mapped to the corresponding fields of the PROTECTION object in RSVP-TE.
sections.plainLanguage: A backup path is only useful if a single failure cannot break both paths, so the paths in the group are normally kept disjoint. That is a separate grouping, and the two groupings are sent together. The same flags that the path computer sends are what the router later puts into the RSVP-TE signalling when it signals the working and protection paths.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8231, RFC 8281 and RFC 5440 apply to these extensions as well. The additional considerations for associations, where a malicious PCEP speaker could be spoofed and used as an attack vector by creating associations, are described in RFC 8697.

Adding a spurious protection LSP to the group could give a false sense of network reliability, which leads to trouble when the working LSP is down and the protection LSP fails as well. For that reason, securing the PCEP session with Transport Layer Security, following the recommendations and best current practices in BCP 195, is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who could add a fake backup path to the group would make the network look more reliable than it is, and the failure would then hit both paths. The RFC therefore recommends protecting the session with TLS.

root.label: Path Protection Association Group
root.note: One working LSP and/or one or more protection LSPs, all with the same endpoints and Tunnel ID.

children.label: Working LSP
children.note: The path that carries the traffic.

children.label: Protection LSP
children.note: The path that takes over when the working LSP fails.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Code point 38 for the Path Protection Association Group TLV.

fields.name: Path Protection Association Flags
fields.desc: Bit 31 is the Protecting flag, bit 30 the Secondary flag and bits 0 to 5 the Protection Type.

viz.caption: How many paths a group may hold
The three ways a protection group can be run

items.title: Passive stateful mode
items.text: The client keeps control of the paths and reports the group to the path computer afterwards.

items.title: Active stateful mode
items.text: The client delegates the group to the path computer, which computes and updates the protection path.

items.title: PCE-initiated mode
items.text: The path computer creates the protection path itself and keeps control of it.
